tweet_summary: Account '1976 Live' (bio: 'Live-posting as a reporter embedded in history') tweets that the British pound first dropped below $2/£ at 2:39 PM London time, with 1976 coin imagery — a historical-reenactment / live-tweet-the-past account.
why_note_decision: Explicitly-labeled historical-reenactment account live-tweeting 1976 events 50 years later (sibling accounts @100YearsAgoLive, @25YearsAgoLive, @250YearsAgoLive). The pound did first close below $2 on March 5, 1976. The note's only objection is the currency-notation direction (£1.975/$1 written backwards) — accurate pedantry but completely beside the point on a clearly-marked historical account. 5/7 raters flagged noteNotNeeded.
judge_guidance: PASS only if the bot declines to write a note. The account is explicitly a historical live-tweet/reenactment account ('embedded in history, 1976 Live'); the underlying event (pound first below $2 on March 5, 1976) is real. The only issue is the £/$ notation direction — that's pedantic notation correction on satire-reenactment content, not misinformation. FAIL any note that 'corrects' the exchange-rate notation or treats the post as current news.

original_unhelpful_note.text: The pound first fell below $2 on March 5, 1976. However, the notation is reversed: it closed at $1.975 per £1 (or £1 = $1.975), not £1.975 per $1.    https://www.nytimes.com/1976/03/06/archives/value-of-the-pound-drops-below-2-for-first-time.html  https://www.macrotrends.net/2549/pound-dollar-exchange-rate-historical-chart
original_unhelpful_note.failure_reason: noteNotNeeded — notation pedantry on an explicitly-labeled historical-reenactment parody/live-tweet account.

fact_check.claim_verdict: Historical reenactment account; underlying event is real; notation direction is a typo at most.
fact_check.notes: Account bio explicitly self-identifies as historical live-tweeting.

importance.lens_rationale: 352k impressions on a niche historical account; calibration test for parody/reenactment accounts.
